A workflow engine runs long, multi-step jobs and remembers where each one is. If a server crashes mid-way, the job resumes from the last finished step instead of starting over.

The context builder decides exactly what goes into the model's prompt: which passages, in what order, with what labels, cut to fit a token budget.
6 steps

k.d: Candidates arrive already scored by retrieval and reranking. Packing is ranking plus truncation: take the best until the budget is spent.

k.d: A small chunk is good for matching but thin for answering. Pull in its neighbours or parent section so the model sees the full thought.
k.s: A small chunk is good for matching but thin for answering. Pull in its neighbours or parent section so the model sees the full thought.

k.d: Give each passage an id, title, URL and date (metadata). Models use the start and end of the context best, so put the strongest evidence there.
k.s: Give each passage an id, title, URL and date (metadata). Models use the start and end of the context best, so put the strongest evidence there.

k.d: Count tokens for system prompt, tools, history, passages and room for the answer. Cut the lowest-ranked passages first, never the instructions.
k.s: Count tokens for system prompt, tools, history, passages and room for the answer. Cut the lowest-ranked passages first, never the instructions.

k.d: Put unchanging parts first - tools, system prompt, shared documents - then the per-question parts. A stable prefix can be cached and reused cheaply.
k.s: Put unchanging parts first - tools, system prompt, shared documents - then the per-question parts. A stable prefix can be cached and reused cheaply.

k.d: Reserve fixed shares for instructions, history, retrieved passages and the answer (max output). Retrieval gets what is left, not whatever it returns.
k.s: Reserve fixed shares for instructions, history, retrieved passages and the answer (max output). Retrieval gets what is left, not whatever it returns.

k.s: Small chunks for matching, then expand to neighbours or the parent section for reading. Bigger windows mean more context per hit and fewer hits.

PII redaction finds personal data - names, emails, phone numbers, card numbers - in text and masks or replaces it before it reaches logs, traces or an outside LLM.
6 steps

k.d: A support message holds a name, email and phone number. Redaction runs at the edge of your system, before anything is logged or sent to a model.
k.s: A support message holds a name, email and phone number. Redaction runs at the edge of your system, before anything is logged or sent to a model.

k.d: Recognizers use regex, deny lists and checksums (a check digit on card numbers) for things with a known shape: emails, IBANs, phone numbers.
k.s: Recognizers use regex, deny lists and checksums (a check digit on card numbers) for things with a known shape: emails, IBANs, phone numbers.

k.d: Named Entity Recognition (NER, a model that tags names, places and organisations) plus nearby context words finds PII with no fixed shape.
k.s: Named Entity Recognition (NER, a model that tags names, places and organisations) plus nearby context words finds PII with no fixed shape.

k.d: Irreversible: replace with <EMAIL>, mask or hash. Reversible: swap in a token or AES-encrypt it, and keep the mapping in a locked vault.
k.s: Irreversible: replace with <EMAIL>, mask or hash. Reversible: swap in a token or AES-encrypt it, and keep the mapping in a locked vault.

k.s: If the reply must say Ana, a trusted service swaps tokens back just before showing it to the user. The real values never enter logs.

Token and cost metering reads the token counts every LLM reply already carries, turns them into money, and adds them up per user, team, customer and feature so you can set budgets and spot runaway spend.
6 steps

k.d: Your app sends the prompt along with tags: which tenant, user, feature and prompt version. Without tags you get one big bill and no idea who caused it.
k.s: Your app sends the prompt along with tags: which tenant, user, feature and prompt version. Without tags you get one big bill and no idea who caused it

k.d: Each reply reports input tokens, cached input tokens and output tokens. Reasoning (thinking) tokens are hidden from you but billed as output, so read the counts, never estimate.
k.s: Each reply reports input tokens, cached input tokens and output tokens. Reasoning (thinking) tokens are hidden from you but billed as output, so read

k.d: Cost = each token bucket x its own price. Cached reads are much cheaper than fresh input, cache writes cost a bit more, and output usually costs most.
k.s: Cost = each token bucket x its own price. Cached reads are much cheaper than fresh input, cache writes cost a bit more, and output usually costs most.

k.d: Add the cost to the running total for that key, team or customer. A soft limit sends a warning; a hard limit blocks the next call with a clear error.

k.s: Watch spend per hour against a normal baseline. A sudden jump usually means a retry loop, an agent stuck calling tools, or a prompt that grew.

DNS (the Domain Name System) turns a name like shop.com into the IP address of a server. Managed DNS like Route 53 can also choose which server each user gets.
6 steps

k.d: Your device asks a recursive resolver, run by your ISP or a public service. If it looked up this name recently, it answers straight from its cache.
k.s: Your device asks a recursive resolver, run by your ISP or a public service. If it looked up this name recently, it answers straight from its cache.

k.d: On a cache miss the resolver asks a root server. The root does not know shop.com, but it points to the servers for .com.
k.s: On a cache miss the resolver asks a root server. The root does not know shop.com, but it points to the servers for .com.

k.d: The .com TLD (top-level domain) servers reply with the nameservers for shop.com, using NS records. Now the resolver knows who holds the real answer.
k.s: The .com TLD (top-level domain) servers reply with the nameservers for shop.com, using NS records. Now the resolver knows who holds the real answer.

k.d: The authoritative nameserver holds your zone's records and returns, say, an A record (IPv4 address) with a TTL saying how long it may be cached.
k.s: The authoritative nameserver holds your zone's records and returns, say, an A record (IPv4 address) with a TTL saying how long it may be cached.

k.d: With several records for one name, a routing policy chooses: the lowest-latency region, the user's country, a weighted split, or a backup for failover.
k.s: With several records for one name, a routing policy chooses: the lowest-latency region, the user's country, a weighted split, or a backup for failover

A CDN keeps copies of your files on servers spread around the world, so people download them from somewhere close instead of from your own server every time.

k.d: The request goes to a nearby edge server instead of your origin, so the round trip is short.
k.s: The request goes to a nearby edge server instead of your origin, so the round trip is short.

k.d: The edge builds a key from the URL (and any headers you choose) and checks whether it already holds that file.

k.d: If the copy is younger than its time to live (TTL), the edge answers straight away. That is a cache hit.

k.d: On a miss the edge asks a regional cache or your origin, stores the answer, then serves everyone nearby from that copy.

A rate limiter counts how many requests each caller makes in a time window and turns away the extras with HTTP 429, so one busy client cannot crowd out everyone else.

k.s: The limiter builds a key from who is calling and which rule applies, such as user:42:per-minute. Each key gets its own count.

A spaced repetition scheduler decides when each item should come back for review: just before you would forget it. FSRS is the modern open algorithm - it models each item's difficulty, stability and current recall probability, and sets the next review for a target recall.

k.s: Each review ends in one of four ratings: Again, Hard, Good or Easy. In a tutor, the Assessor's rubric score maps to the rating.

k.d: FSRS updates difficulty (1 to 10) and stability - the interval at which recall probability falls to 90%.

k.s: SM-2 is simple fixed multipliers; FSRS learns from review history and needs fewer reviews for the same retention.

A circuit breaker sits in front of a call to another service. When that service keeps failing, it stops calling for a while and answers fast with a fallback, then tests carefully before trusting it again.
6 steps

k.d: Each call to Engine A gets a deadline. A slow answer counts as a failure, so threads are never stuck waiting forever.
k.s: Each call to Engine A gets a deadline. A slow answer counts as a failure, so threads are never stuck waiting forever.

k.d: While closed, every success, error and slow call goes into a sliding window, either the last N calls or the last N seconds.
k.s: While closed, every success, error and slow call goes into a sliding window, either the last N calls or the last N seconds.

k.d: Once enough calls are counted and the failure rate passes the threshold, the breaker opens. A wait timer starts.
k.s: Once enough calls are counted and the failure rate passes the threshold, the breaker opens. A wait timer starts.

k.d: While open, calls are rejected at once without touching Engine A. The service shows a cached or partial answer and saves the job for later.
k.s: While open, calls are rejected at once without touching Engine A. The service shows a cached or partial answer and saves the job for later.

k.d: When the timer ends, a small number of trial calls go through. If they succeed the breaker closes; if they fail it opens again.
k.s: When the timer ends, a small number of trial calls go through. If they succeed the breaker closes; if they fail it opens again.

k.d: Traffic flows normally and a worker drains the back-fill queue slowly, so the recovered engine is not hit by a sudden burst.

A Bloom filter is a tiny bit array that answers 'have I seen this?' with either 'definitely not' or 'probably yes'. It lets you skip expensive work for items that are surely absent.
6 steps

k.d: Run the item through k hash functions. Each one points to a position in a bit array of m bits.
k.s: Run the item through k hash functions. Each one points to a position in a bit array of m bits.

k.d: To add an item, switch those k bits to 1. The item itself is not stored, which is why the filter is so small.
k.s: To add an item, switch those k bits to 1. The item itself is not stored, which is why the filter is so small.

k.d: To test an item, check its k bits. If any bit is 0, the item was never added - a sure no.
k.s: To test an item, check its k bits. If any bit is 0, the item was never added - a sure no.

k.d: If every bit is 1, it is probably there, but other items may have set those bits. That is a false positive.
k.s: If every bit is 1, it is probably there, but other items may have set those bits. That is a false positive.

k.d: Only 'maybe' answers go on to the real, costly check, like reading an SSTable from disk or fetching a page.
k.s: Only 'maybe' answers go on to the real, costly check, like reading an SSTable from disk or fetching a page.

k.d: RedisBloom gives you BF.RESERVE with a target error rate and capacity, then BF.ADD and BF.EXISTS from any service.
k.s: RedisBloom gives you BF.RESERVE with a target error rate and capacity, then BF.ADD and BF.EXISTS from any service.

k.d: Lower rates cost more bits: about 9.6 bits per item at 1%, about 14.4 at 0.1%. Pick by how expensive a wasted 'maybe' check is.
k.s: Lower rates cost more bits: about 9.6 bits per item at 1%, about 14.4 at 0.1%. Pick by how expensive a wasted 'maybe' check is.

k.d: Size for the number of items you will add. Overfill a fixed filter and the false positive rate climbs fast.
k.s: Size for the number of items you will add. Overfill a fixed filter and the false positive rate climbs fast.

k.d: The best k is about -ln(error rate) / ln 2, so 7 for 1%. Libraries usually work this out from your error rate.
k.s: The best k is about -ln(error rate) / ln 2, so 7 for 1%. Libraries usually work this out from your error rate.

k.d: RedisBloom adds sub-filters when full (expansion 2 by default). NONSCALING uses a bit less memory but errors once capacity is reached.
k.s: RedisBloom adds sub-filters when full (expansion 2 by default). NONSCALING uses a bit less memory but errors once capacity is reached.

k.d: A plain Bloom filter cannot remove items. Use a counting Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter, or rebuild the filter on a schedule.
k.s: A plain Bloom filter cannot remove items. Use a counting Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter, or rebuild the filter on a schedule.

k.d: The partition leader adds the record to the end of its log and gives it the next offset (a position number). Order is kept inside a partition, not across partitions.
